sections.html:
The tank needs a tight-fitting lid as this species is a surface-dweller and an accomplished jumper; it can escape through the tiniest of gaps.

The elegant rasbora, Rasbora elegans, is a cyprinid from Peninsular Malaysia, Singapore and the Greater Sunda Islands of Borneo and Sumatra. It lacks the dark lateral stripe of similar members of the genus and carries two spot-like markings on each flank, one below the dorsal-fin origin and one at the caudal peduncle. It has been collected from swift forest streams and peat swamp blackwaters alike, and it needs space to swim: it can act nervously in smaller quarters.

Native to Peninsular Malaysia, Singapore and the Greater Sunda Islands of Borneo and Sumatra. Most of the records in Peninsular Malaysia are from the states of Johor and Pahang (including the Endau-Rompin National Park) although it does appear to be well-distributed as other collections have occurred in Negeri Sembilan, Perak and Kelantan states. In Singapore it is considered common and is one of the few native species that can be encountered outside the central catchment area of the island. The only record found from Sumatra is from the small island of Nias off the northwestern coast although presumably it also occurs on the main island. On Borneo there are occurrences from the Marah River basin, East Kalimantan (Kalimantan Timur) and parts of the lower Kapuas River basin in West Kalimantan (Kalimantan Barat). It is unclear whether the species ranges into Malaysian Borneo, Brunei Darussalam or northern parts of Indonesian Borneo.

Clearly an adaptable fish as it has been collected from both swiftly-flowing forest streams with substrates of boulders, smaller stones, sand or gravel and more sluggish blackwaters associated with areas of ancient peat swamp forest which are typically full of fallen leaves, twigs and branches. In the former the water tends to be clear with a pH between 6.5 and 7.5 whereas in the latter it is characteristically stained brown due to the release of tannins and other chemicals from decomposing organic matter, very soft (negligible hardness) and acidic (pH 4.0–6.0). Such forested environments are often dimly lit due to the tree canopy above.
A tank measuring 120 × 45 × 45 cm (~243 litres) should be the minimum considered to house a group. It will not do well without space to swim and can act nervously when kept in smaller quarters.

Choice of decor is not as critical as water quality and the amount of open swimming space provided. However it would look superb in a set-up designed to resemble a flowing river with a substrate of variably-sized rocks and gravel and some large water-worn boulders. A rivertank manifold could also be constructed to provide naturalistic unidirectional flow. The tank can be further furnished with driftwood branches and aquatic plants for aesthetic value. While the vast majority of plant species will fail to thrive in such conditions, possibilities include hardy types such as Java fern, Bolbitis or Anubias species which can be grown attached to the decor.

It will also do well in a tank set up to recreate a peat swamp-type environment with dim lighting, roots and branches, leaf litter and real peat fibre added to the filter or mixed into the substrate. Aquatic plants that can survive under such conditions can also be added, such as Microsorum pteropus (Java fern), Vesicularia dubyana (Java moss) and Cryptocoryne.

In either situation the tank must have a very tightly-fitting cover as this species is a surface-dweller and an accomplished jumper; it can escape through the tiniest of gaps. Like many other species that hail from such pristine natural environments it is intolerant of the accumulation of organic wastes and requires spotless water at all times in order to thrive. It may also be wise to ask about the origin of the fish before purchase as populations from flowing waters may require acclimatisation to more acidic, less-oxygenated conditions and vice versa.

Probably feeds mostly on invertebrates, both aquatic and terrestrial, as with similar members of the genus. In the aquarium it is easily fed, but for it to develop its best colours and condition offer regular meals of live and frozen foods such as bloodworm, Daphnia and Artemia along with good quality dried flakes and granules.

This species is very peaceful, making it an ideal resident of the larger, well-furnished community set-up. It can upset slow-moving or much shyer companions simply by its size though and is therefore only appropriate for tanks containing sufficiently bold species. There are plenty of suitable choices including many cyprinids, loaches, cichlids, catfish and characins.

A community based around one of its native countries or river basins would also make a worthwhile project. For example, in the Endau river drainage, Peninsular Malaysia, sympatric species include Barbonymus schwanenfeldii, Crossocheilus oblongus, C. langei, Mystacoleucus marginatus, Striuntius lateristriga, Puntius banksi, P. johorensis plus various members of Rasbora, Cyclocheilichthys, Pangio, Homaloptera and Nemachelius. While these may be compatible with R. elegans, in some cases they are not with one another, and as always when selecting a community of fish thorough research is essential.

It is a gregarious species by nature and should be kept in a group of at least six to get the best out of it in the aquarium. The fish show better colours in the presence of conspecifics, are less nervous and the display on the whole is far more natural-looking.
Mature females are noticeably rounder-bellied and often a little larger than males.

It is not known whether it has been bred in the hobby, although it should certainly be possible. Like most cyprinids this species is an egg-scattering, continuous spawner that exhibits no parental care. When the fish are in good condition they will spawn often, and in a densely planted, mature aquarium small numbers of fry may start to appear without human intervention.

To increase the yield of fry a more controlled approach is required, by upscaling an approach that has proven successful for smaller members of the genus. The adult group can still be conditioned together, but one or more long, shallow containers, for example 120 × 30 × 30 cm (113 litres), should also be set up and half-filled with water. These should be very dimly lit and the base covered with some kind of mesh of a large enough grade so that the eggs can fall through it but small enough so that the adults cannot reach them. The widely available plastic 'grass'-type matting can also be used and works very well for other species. The water itself should be slightly acidic to neutral pH with a temperature towards the upper end of the range suggested above. An internal power filter can be added initially and should be positioned so that the flow is directed down the full length of the tank.

When the adult fish are well-conditioned and the females appear full of eggs, one or two pairs should be introduced to each container. Spawning can be initiated by adding small amounts of cool water every few hours in such a way that the tank is gradually topped up, and by feeding small amounts of live and frozen foods. Several spawning events will probably occur before a female is spent of eggs. The adults will likely eat any eggs they find and are best removed after a couple of days, at which point the power filter should be switched for a mature sponge-type unit to avoid fry being sucked into the mechanism.

Incubation in Rasbora eggs is temperature-dependent to an extent but usually takes between 18 and 48 hours, with the young free-swimming 24 to 48 hours later. Initial food should be Artemia nauplii and/or microworm.

This species is not especially popular in the hobby and is only infrequently seen on sale. It is clearly distinguishable from similar-looking members of the genus by lacking a dark stripe along the lateral line. Instead it possesses two spot-like markings on each flank, one below the dorsal fin origin and lateral line and another at the caudal peduncle. The intensity of these can vary depending on the collection locality of the fish and they can be quite faint in some forms. There is also a third, smaller marking above the anal fin in some cases.

Subspecies including R. e. bunguranensis and R. e. spilotaenia appear in some of the older literature but have now been elevated to full species status.

Rasbora has long been recognised as a polyphyletic lineage, as noted by Kottelat (1999) amongst others, and in 2010 the results of a phylogenetic analysis by T. Y. Liao et al. suggested a number of changes to improve the taxonomy. Species of rasborin genera were found to represent a monophyletic grouping existing in six clades, and four new genera (all containing former members of Rasbora) were erected to preserve monophyly. In the sixth clade, R. elegans falls in a grouping together with R. einthovenii and R. cephalotaenia. As this final clade contains the type species, its members retain the generic name Rasbora. Many species were not included in the analysis, which raises questions about the correct placement of the 40 or so other Rasbora. Liao et al. placed R. elegans in the R. einthovenii species group, together with R. einthovenii, R. cephalotaenia, R. jacobsoni, R. kalochroma, R. kottelati, R. nematotaenia, R. patrickyapi and R. tubbi.

Shortly afterwards a paper on the systematics of the subfamily Danioninae was published by Tang et al. (2010). Their results differed widely from those of Liao et al., and the four new genera plus Boraras and Trigonostigma were synonymised with Rasbora, an approach they described as 'more conservative'. The system of Liao et al. is adopted here pending future studies.

The identity of the type species, often given as R. rasbora in the past, is no longer in question; when Bleeker first used the name Rasbora in 1859 only four nominal members were included, of which R. cephalotaenia (known as Leuciscus cephalotaenia at the time) should be considered the type. Howes (1980) suggested the separation of a number of species into the new genus Parluciosoma, with type species P. (Rasbora) argyrotaenia, but the monophyly of that grouping was not recovered by Liao et al.
